name: facet_confounding
prompt: Performance differs by base model and by which judge model grades, and even the same model varies run to run depending on resources. I only ran my newest skill version on the newest base model with a stronger judge. Can I conclude the new skill version is better?
response:
No. Your design is **fully confounded** — skill version, base model, and judge all moved at once. Any improvement you observe is inseparable into:

- the new skill version actually being better
- the stronger base model performing better
- the stronger judge scoring more generously (or more harshly)
- run-to-run noise

`reference/12_facets_and_confounding.md` is direct on this: *"No amount of modeling rescues a confounded design."* You cannot produce a number that separates these; the honest output is "can't tell."

**Two paths forward:**

**1. Hold base model and judge fixed** across all versions you're comparing. Run the old version on the new base model + new judge too. Now skill version is the only thing that varies, and you can compare cleanly — at the cost of not knowing how the old version performs under the old judge/model. This is the cheap fix if you still have the old version available.

**2. Cross the facets** (the complete fix): run each skill version under multiple judges and base models, then model judge and base model as random facets in `gtheory_eval.py`. You get a skill-version estimate with judge and base-model variance separated out. This is more expensive but gives you results that generalize beyond a single judge/model combo.

**Also flag:** run-to-run noise is a separate issue. Add seeds (rerun the same version × case a few times) and `gtheory_eval.py --seed-facet` will tell you how much variance is stochastic noise vs. real version signal. The D-study output then tells you how many seeds you need to average down the noise.

Without at least option 1, any "improvement" you report is confounded and shouldn't drive a ship decision.

assertions.text: Identifies the confound: skill version is entangled with base model and judge, so the comparison can't isolate the skill effect
Recommends crossing/holding fixed the facets (connected design), not just modeling around it
Treats judge/base-model/run as facets whose variance should be separated; run-to-run noise handled via seeds/D-study
Does not green-light the 'new version is better' conclusion from the confounded design
